text: Every warehouse table you've touched this chapter falls into one of exactly two roles. Time to name them properly: fact tables and dimension tables.

A fact table holds measurable events — things that happened, with numbers attached. Mostly foreign keys, plus a handful of measures you'd sum or average. Narrow, but potentially millions of rows tall. A dimension table holds the descriptive context around those events — who, what, when, where. Wide, but relatively few rows.
Fact Internet Sales is the textbook fact table. Almost nothing but keys pointing at dimensions, plus sales amount and order quantity — the actual numbers worth adding up.

Dim Product is the textbook dimension. Product name, color, size, list price — rich, descriptive attributes you'd group or filter by, not sum. Put the two together with a join, and you get real answers: what happened, and what it actually means.

Fact tables narrow and tall, dimension tables wide and short — on purpose, because of how many rows each one actually holds. Next lesson: how these two shapes connect together into a schema — the star schema. See you there.
